articles.description:
Every so often I suffer from what I call "Emacs Fatigue". It's closely related to "Text File Fatigue". Using Emacs tends to pull one toward using it for everything, which is what I'd done. Then, I simply grow tired of staring at the same thing every day. When this happens, I "decide" to uproot my life and move my notes into something else. This time, that something else was Bear.
Bear is great. It's solid, beautiful, and refreshingly simple. It syncs flawlessly (for free) and runs on macOS and iOS. It's also inexpensive. It uses an SQLite database, which doesn't bother me. Databases are great at this stuff. All the "But but what if the database...?!" talk is mostly hearsay anyway.
The thing that made me twitchy was that it felt like my notes were "in there". It's not the database. It's the fact that everything is in an app, and that app makes me need to use that app. This is how I'd started to feel about Emacs, but mostly due to Org mode.
Bear is macOS and iOS only, which should be fine for someone like me who has "decided" to live on macOS. And yet, Linux continues to emit a low-grade hum in the back of my head that I can't ignore.
If I don't want my notes in Org mode files, but I'm still drawn toward Emacs, what should I do? Denote! That's where they'd all started in the first place, but as .org not .md. I'd nearly forgotten that Denote handles Markdown files natively. One Emacs configuration change and I was back where I belong. And since Bear notes are already Markdown, all it took was an export and a (Claude Code-assisted) conversion script for file names, links, and attachments.
So yes, I've done that thing where I quit using Emacs only to come crawling back later. I know better, but knowing better doesn't stop me. Maybe I'll work on a sync/bridge between Denote and Bear. That would be neat.

articles.description:
I was on my Mac this morning, just minding my own business, when suddenly I found myself using the Linux laptop, and I liked it.
On Sunday mornings, I do system maintenance. This means running updates on all my computers. Right now, that's five machines: one Linux desktop, two Linux laptops, one Mac desktop, and one Mac laptop. Yes, that's too many, but it is what it is.
Both Linux laptops run CachyOS, which is Arch-based, so there are always updates.
I started with the Framework. Once it was updated and rebooted, I pulled the latest tweaks to my Emacs config, to make sure it worked on Linux. I've been leaning toward using macOS exclusively, so I haven't been testing things on Linux as much. Everything worked, though.
While typing on the Framework, the first thing I thought about was how much I prefer typing on it to typing on the MacBook Air. Then I remembered how much I like the idea of Linux. Then I noticed that Emacs starts up more than twice as fast on the Framework for some reason. Then I remembered that the best (and only) way to have consistent Emacs key bindings on Linux is to, well, use Emacs.
All this to say that the conflict between running macOS, Linux, or both is still a thing. As troublesome and complex as it can be, I think the answer will always be "both". Surely I can manage it, right? Maybe if I only use the laptops for simple things like blogging, browsing, or journaling, things will be easy enough. I'll never be able to settle on one or the other. Just admit it.
I'm on the couch typing this in Emacs using the Framework, both things I told myself a week ago that I'd stop doing. My stupid brain is always mucking things up.
✍️ Reply by email

articles.description:
littleFedi is "A small ActivityPub server written in Go"
It was officially released (I think) yesterday, and is another project from Stefano Marinelli of BSSG fame.
A few years ago I'd decided I wanted to "own my content" 🙄 so I ran an instance of Mastodon. Mastodon is overkill and I didn't enjoy it. Then, later, I installed an instance of Go2Social, which worked well. Trouble was, I was all-in with social media at the time and being on a single-user instance felt lonely...nothing useful in "local" or "trending". Discovery was difficult. It was just me and I didn't like it.
Fast forward to today, and things have changed. I've deleted all of my Meta-related accounts and LinkedIn. I thought about quitting Mastodon as well, but FOMO always gets the better of me.
Since I would rather not quit Mastodon completely, I figured I would try running a single-user instance again. Maybe the quiet would be good for me.
I'd seen @Stefano's posts about a new ActivityPub server he was working on and the timing of the first release couldn't be better, so I installed it today at Jack Baty Social.

It's running on my Hetzner VPS behind Caddy as a proxy. I love Caddy. Here's the entire Caddy config for the domain:
social.baty.net {
	encode gzip
	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8081
}

I've just started poking around, but littleFedi seems like it's got a lot going for it. At first I wanted to use my root domain for my handle (@jack@baty.net) but since I'd previously used that via Ghost, I ran into caching issues and didn't want to bother, so now I'm @jack@social.baty.net.
The big question is whether to migrate followers there, or start fresh and maybe just announce the move from my main @jbaty@social.lol account. I think I'll give it a minute before deciding.
littleFedi is a compelling new entry in the FediverseSpaceArena.

articles.description:
Will voice kill the keyboard. No. Will the way we interact with Emacs, and computers in general, change drastically? No.
Star Trek has a mythical AI/computer that responds to voice commands and interacts with you to clarify or note other work that may pertain to what you wanted. Evidently the interface is so ubiquitous that Scotty talks to a mouse noting it's "quaint" to need to push it and type on a keyboard to interact with a computer.
But if we watch the bridge of any Star Trek show people aren't talking the whole time. They're tapping screens to get the computer to do things for them. Theoretically the captain could tell the ship where he wants to go and let the computer do it, but he issues a command and then someone types in the needed commands to the ship so it goes in the expected direction.
I work at home in a solo office space. I could talk to my computer and it would disturb no one, except me. I'd be unable to listen to music on my stereo at the same time just in case the computer couldn't understand my words versus the song.
I don't think keyboards are going anywhere any time soon. They provide an unambiguous interface to your computer that doesn't disturb others. I think that those loving Emacs interactions like they use it will continue to do so as they do now because it's the most efficient way to control the Emacs interface.
articles.title: Curtis McHale: Emacs Carnival - Will we change how we interact with Emacs?

articles.description:
very nice solution to a problem posed by David Pape: how can we enter a range of numbers as list of distinct numbers in Emacs? Pape’s specific problem was entering the numbers of error reports that a Git commit closes. Rather than entering something like

closes: 47, 48, 49, 50, 51, 70


he’d like to enter something like

closes: 47-51 70


and call an Emacs function to have it expanded into the first example.


Chua has a very nice solution that covers that case as well things like

47-51, 70


or even

5-15/2


to expand into the sequence

5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15


Most of the heavy lifting is done by the number-sequence function. The rest of the work is parsing the input string into either a single number or a range of numbers that number-sequence can work on.


Chua’s solution strikes me as an example of Emacs at its best. The problem it solves is not earth shattering. It’s simply a bit of friction in a user’s everyday workflow but Emacs easily provides a solution that makes the friction disappear. Take a look at her code. It not only shows an ingenious solution to the problem but also demonstrates the power of Emacs and Elisp to make the application of that genius simple.
articles.title: Irreal: Inserting Number Ranges As A List

articles.description:
extolling the power of plain text. It’s a notion that’s familiar to all us Emacs users and even more so to Org users. We Org users (or more generally Markdown and other markup users) can write plain text and have it formatted for output in a variety of ways. The point is, the text stays text and is readable even without the formatting.


As nickb says, text written today will still be readable 50 years from now. Sure, UTF-8 and the other Unicode formats can and do add new characters from time to time but text written today will have the same meaning even if new characters are added.


The most important aspect is that you’ll own your data no matter what programs come and go. Emacs isn’t going anywhere but even if it did, it wouldn’t matter. Text will still be readable and something like Org or Markdown will still make intended formatting obvious even if Org and Markdown no longer exist.


Nickb acknowledges that text is not the right answer for everything. You wouldn’t, for example, want to represent a photograph in plain text and there are lots of other examples. Still, for many applications, plain text is not only sufficient but probably the better solution.

articles.description:
David Pape asked:




I just typed



>Closes: #47, #48, #49, #50, #51, #52, #53, #54



into a commit description, all by hand.



Is there a way in Emacs to expand some kind of range description to make this easier? 😅



I want to expand strings like "5-10, 15-18, 3" into numbers.




Hmm, could be useful. It reminds me of how page ranges work, which will be handy if I want to tinker with PDFs. Let's see if something like this works:




(defun sacha-parse-page-range (s)
  "Parse a page range string and return a list of numbers.
Ex: 1-5
2-4, 6-10
1 4 7-9
3-11/2   - this one specifies an increment"
  (seq-mapcat
   (lambda (part)
     (let ((nums (mapcar 'string-to-number (split-string part " *[-/] *"))))
       (if (= (length nums) 1)
           nums
         (number-sequence (elt nums 0) (elt nums 1) (elt nums 2)))))
   (split-string s "[, \t\n\r]+")))

(ert-deftest sacha-parse-page-range ()
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "5-10")
                 '(5 6 7 8 9 10)))
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "1-5, 8")
                 '(1 2 3 4 5 8)))
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "1 4 7-9")
                 '(1 4 7 8 9)))
  (should (equal (sacha-parse-page-range "3-11/2")
                 '(3 5 7 9 11))))

(defun sacha-issue-range (range)
  "Expand RANGE to a list of issues and insert them."
  (interactive "MRange (ex: 1-5, 7): ")
  (let ((s (mapconcat (lambda (n) (format "#%d" n))
                      (sacha-parse-page-range range)
                      ", ")))
    (when (called-interactively-p 'any)
      (insert s))
    s))

This is part of my EmacsConfiguration.

articles.description:
A long-standing passion of mine is listening to and collecting music. I’m always on the lookout for new music and where I discover it is primarily from internet radio stations. That said, listening to music in such a way is largely a passive activity, where your main focus is somewhere else. The better music players that acknowledge this difference in focus provide mechanisms for remote-controlling them from other apps. So it is with the Triode app for macOS, which leverages Cocoa frameworks (App Intents in particular) to support remote control.
triode.el is an Emacs Lisp library which provides a simple remote control interface to the Triode app. Basic support for selecting a radio station, play/stop, and muting are provided. Not every feature in the Triode app is accessible to triode.el though; this is controlled by the App Intents actually implemented by its developer, The Iconfactory.

Interested readers can learn more about triode.el in its user guide.
triode.el is now available on MELPA. This release joins my other packages that support remote control of music apps on macOS from Emacs:
now-playing.el - Interface for the Music app.
shazam.el - Interface for Shazam music recognition.
All the above efforts have been an exploration of malleable computing using Emacs as the main orchestration tool. I plan on posting a more technical deep dive reflecting this work in the not too distant future. That said, if you’re a macOS user who uses Emacs and Triode, I encourage you to give triode.el a try. Also, consider this a plug for Triode app, a well-designed app that does a great job of taking advantage of the Cocoa frameworks to provide internet radio across different devices provided by Apple.

articles.description:
What’s the future of Emacs? He asks that question in the context of assuming that Emacs will continue to exist for any timeline that matters to us. But how, he asks, will we use it?


The answer that will occur to most of us is speech mediated input á la Star Trek TNG. We’ll simply tell Emacs what we want it to do and it will do it. But think about that for a moment. Would you really want to dictate the code for your latest program to the computer? Or would you even want to dictate your documentation, story, or letter to your computer?


Sure, you could say something like, “Computer write a program to do such and such.” but then you’re not using Emacs at all. The same for asking the computer to write something for you. That—more or less—is here today but most of us don’t like the results and, again, we’re not really using Emacs in those situations.


For my part, my written thoughts are always much better organized than my spoken ones so even with  capable voice input, I’d much prefer to use the keyboard. Maiorana agrees. He points back to a couple of episodes from Tales From the Darkside1 in which people use the keyboard to do magic with the computer. For him, Meta+x is the spell that enables the magic and he’s very attached to it. Like me, he doesn’t anticipate abandoning the keyboard.


What do you think? Will we still use the keyboard or will we move on to something better?


Footnotes: 
1 



You can find Mookie and Pookie and Word Processor of the Gods in the Internet Archive.

articles.description:
informative post from Ankit Gadiya about unwanted nested frames in Emacs. The TL;DR is that Gadiya runs Ghostel as his Emacs shell in TUI and demon mode. That works well but he has a script that calls emacsclient to load a file. There’s nothing special about it; it’s just what you’d expect it to be but when he runs it from with Ghostel, it creates a nested frame in the Ghostel frame rather than replacing the Ghostel frame.


The solution is pretty simple. Gadiya changed his script to check if he was in Ghostel, and if so, calls emacsclient with a parameter to reuse the current frame. You can check Gadiya’s post for the details.


For me, the most interesting aspect was how he checked if he was in Ghostel. It turns out that Emacs sets the environment variable INSIDE_EMACS when it’s running a shell or subprocess. I didn’t know that so I learned something new from Gadiya’s post.


Update [2026-10-05 Mon 11:15]: Added link to Gadiya’s post.

articles.description:
Earlier this year I added Ghostel to my
Emacs configuration. Ghostel is a terminal emulator for Emacs that uses
Ghostty's engine underneath. It is a delight to use
especially with the TUI applications.
Nested Emacs frame problem
I use Emacs in daemon
mode,
and then use emacsclient to open new frames from the daemon. To use the same
Emacs daemon when opening files through other programs such as git, sops, I have
a small shell script ee configured as my default EDITOR. It opens a new
Emacs frame in the terminal.
#!/bin/sh

exec emacsclient --create-frame --no-window-system "$@"

When I run this script from Ghostel, it opens a nested Emacs frame in Ghostel's
terminal session.

Solution
Emacs sets an environment variable INSIDE_EMACS for shells and subprocesses.
The script use this variable to check if it is launched from Ghostel and use the
--reuse-frame flag to open the new buffer in the current frame.
#!/bin/sh

if [ "$INSIDE_EMACS" = "ghostel" ]
then
  exec emacsclient --reuse-frame "$@"
fi

exec emacsclient --create-frame --no-window-system "$@"
articles.title: Ankit Gadiya: Fix nested Emacs frames

articles.description:
What is spook?
  The Emacs function spook is
  not what you think it is.  It doesn't make creepy noises, draw scary
  ASCII art or change the theme to orange on black.  In fact it has
  nothing at all to do with Halloween, ghosts, monsters, pandemics or
  IRS audits.



What it does is insert words and phrases into the current buffer "to
help give your message ... attractiveness for automated keyword
scanners."



What kind of words or phrases might you expect to see?  To find out I
invoked spook while composing this content.  Here's what
it added:




    TELINT Drug North Korea Security Consulting Virii Abu Ghraib Fort
    Hancock CUD AMEMB Vaccine MARTA racal E.O.D. Blizzard Nigeria
  



  It's easy1 to configure spook to insert an alternate set
  of words and phrases -- just change the file name in the
  variable spook-phrases-file from "spook.lines" to the
  name of the alternate file.  Unfortunately it must reside in the
  Emacs data directory; the file's location is fixed.  The variable
  can be found in the Spook customization group, whose parent group is
  Games.



  Even with only 72 lines in its source code file,2 spook
demonstrates how to insert one or more random lines from a file into
the current buffer.



  1 It's "easy" if you have Administrator permissions.



  2 The 72 lines is the entire spook.el file; the first 48%
of the file provides the usual comments that describe the GNU GPL,
author, maintainer info as well as documentation.
articles.title: Raymond Zeitler: What is spook?

articles.description:
org-todo is C-c
C-t.  Today I learned about another command with a similar
keybinding (C-c C-x C-t) --
org-toggle-timestamp-overlays.  Note the C-x
in the middle.



When I pressed that key combination (inadvertently), all the
YYYY-MM-DD timestamps in the buffer were converted to the MM/DD/YYYY
format.  This was unacceptable -- I needed to change them back.
However undo did not revert the timestamps; it just undid
the last edit.  Furthermore, these undesired timestamps couldn't be
edited and were impervious to org-shiftright.  I was
confused yet again.



I didn't even know how this happened.  So I
invoked view-lossage as a kind reader once suggested 1
and discovered org-toggle-timestamp-overlays.



The docstring was no help – it's self-evident that it would "Toggle
the use of custom time stamp formats."  Eager to clock out of my task,
I didn't care to learn more.  All I wanted to do was undo the effect.



I figured that since it toggles the timestamp, all I had to do was
invoke it again to toggle it back.  Nope.  Well, a nice message
appears, saying "Time stamp overlays removed."  Yet the timestamps
looked the same.



Undaunted, I figured I'd reload the buffer with org-mode-restart.
That had no effect.  To finally fix this, I deleted the buffer and
revisited the file.



A command like this surely is in the same category as upcase-region,
which is disabled by default.  And so this is why I added
  (put 'org-toggle-timestamp-overlays 'disabled t) to my init file.



  1 See https://ray-on-emacs.blogspot.com/2026/05/emacs-view-commands.html
articles.title: Raymond Zeitler: Now org-toggle-timestamp-overlays is Disabled

articles.description:
Aquí, is sort of a niche application but is potentially useful for more than just its intended use.


The back story is that Choi really likes the sunrise-sunset command in Emacs that tells him the times that the sun rises and sets. The problem is that sunrise-sunset requires that you first specify the latitude and longitude of where you want to know the times. The standard way of doing that is to record them in your init.el, which is what I do. Choi, however, travels with his laptop but still wants to know when the sun is coming up or going down. There’s no automatic way of setting the information so he wrote Aquí to provide it. The only downside is that it works exclusively on the Mac platform.


Once installed, all you need do is call aqui to set all the appropriate information. I hardly ever travel these days so I wasn’t going to bother but it’s easy to use and can give you your current latitude and longitude as well as your address so I thought, “Why not?”. After I installed and ran it, it gave me my exact address as well as my latitude and longitude. That might sometimes vary a bit depending on the vagaries of GPS but it’s certain to be close.


If you decide to try it out, be sure to take a look at the user manual so see what commands are available. Mostly, though, you’ll just need to run aqui. Also be sure to check out the installation section because you need to install a shortcut. That’s just a matter of clicking on a link in the manual but Aquí won’t work until you do.
articles.title: Irreal: Aquí Location Finder

articles.description:
A few days ago I announced
that I am working on denote-data. The goal is to provide an opt-in,
in-memory cache for Denote. It can be used to speed up certain
computationally expensive operations. It must be opt-in because there
are many users, myself included, who do not need such functionality (I
program because the challenge is fun, just how I did with denote-sequence, for example).
I have a final update on this that I posted on denote.git issue 724 
and am copying below. Any future changes will appear in the release
notes of the next version of Denote. In short: it is happening.
The status update on denote.git
Hello again folks!
I have an update on the denote-data project. The code is in this denote.git branch for now: https://github.com/protesilaos/denote/tree/denote-data
What I am doing:
Find the computationaly heavy functions.
Write denote-data variants for them.
Introduce variables to funcall VAR instead of calling the heavy functions directly.
Make the denote-data-mode set those variables.
This way we can have any extension do what denote-data does. And this way denote-data can be its own package as well.
The first big problem I see now is how to make the caching functions async. I will figure this out by studying list-packages and related.
Then I want to study filenotify.el. @mentalisttraceur I have noted that your code is okay for copyright purposes, so I can check it out. Or you can send a PR, if you prefer.
Otherwise, I think this is almost done.
With an opt-in cache we can support other workflows that people have been asking for, such as in-buffer completion.
articles.title: Protesilaos: Emacs: status update on the ‘denote-data’ cache for Denote

articles.description:
One of my favorite Emacs commands is sunrise-sunset (Sunrise/Sunset (GNU Emacs Manual)) to get the day’s times for sunrise and sunset. For it to work right, you must have Emacs pre-configured with location information. This is done by setting three customizable variables:
calendar-latitude
calendar-longitude
calendar-location-name
If you run Emacs on a system that is fixed in location, manually setting the above variables is a one time task. However if you do a fair amount of traveling with Emacs on a laptop, a more programmatic solution might be desired using a location service, ideally an OS-native one. If you’re a macOS user, Aquí (aqui.el) does just that by invoking a Shortcut to query the OS-native location service.
Leveraging Shortcuts gives Emacs access to a high-accuracy fused location update without need to build, install, and configure a separate macOS executable.
Once Aquí is installed, updating the location is done via the aqui command.


1

M-x aqui RET





This will update the above mentioned variables and message the current location in the mini-buffer.
For more information, refer to the Aquí User Guide.
Aquí is now available on MELPA.

articles.description:
wrote back in July, although I’ve had Embark installed for some time, I’ve only just begun to really use it. Most of my uses involve following a link (of any type) and acting on a group of files, typically to delete several files at once. Of course, those uses are barely scratching the surface of Embark’s capabilities.


Those capabilities are essentially open ended. By that I mean you can define your own Embark actions. Stefano Rodighiero has a nice example of this. It’s a nice example for two reasons. First, it’s simple and easy to follow even though—the second reason—I don’t know anything about what he’s trying to do.  The point is that Rodighiero has an obscure—to me—application that he wants to provide an action for but you don’t need to know the details of the application to follow the action.


This is incredibly powerful. Rodighiero let Embark do the hard work of identifying and parsing the target and merely wrote some simple glue to take that target reference and do something useful with it.


If, like me, you’re just beginning to feel your way around Embark, Rodighiero’s post is a useful read. You almost certainly won’t have a need to copy his action but it’s an excellent go by for your own.

articles.description:
Dylan Larkin is still a Red Wing, even though he doesn't want to be. His offseason trade request, arriving after 11 seasons with the club and a mere five playoff games (all as a rookie), symbolized the franchise's inability to shift out of neutral and forced fans to stare the worst-case scenario in the face: After all these years of waiting, maybe the Wings remain closer to the No. 1 draft pick than a playoff run. As the team's second-best goal-scorer and top-line center, Larkin would be impossible to replace quickly, so him deciding that he's given up on this project and would rather just get to the postseason with a contender now that he's in his 30s is a frustrating setback.
It's an issue, too, that has yet to be resolved as the Red Wings wrap their first week of regular season play. The list of teams that Larkin is reportedly willing to waive his no-movement clause for is tiny and elite (not to mention cap-crunched), and Detroit, which doesn't even have a non-interim GM at the moment, has yet to swing a deal. Consequently, Larkin was stripped of his team captaincy, and he got lustily booed by fans when his name was announced on opening night. He sat out the first two losses of the season with injury while the Wings allowed five goals over four-and-a-half periods before they even got on the board. And when he returned to the ice in front of a sad-looking turnout on Tuesday night against Ottawa, those who chose to voice their opinion were generally not happy to see him.
But this game played out differently than the Wings' previous poor showings. While Ottawa got the first goal not even three minutes in, the men in red mounted a meaningful response, scoring four unanswered en route to a 5-3 win. And it was Larkin who played the biggest role of anyone—not as a pariah, but as a talented forward who has consistently injected at least a little bit of light into otherwise dark passages.
articles.title: Dylan Larkin And The Red Wings Are Having Agonizing Breakup Sex On Live TV

articles.description:
The single discordant note in the otherwise effervescent National League Divisional Series between the Milwaukee Brewers and San Diego Padres so far was a brief shot of new Padres owners Jose E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones watching Game 3. It was easy to imagine them, less than two months into the new gig, assuming that it would always be like this. All they know is winning two out of every three games, playing before sold-out houses, and learning cool inside-baseball phrases like "Goddammit, Merrill." They'll find out soon that this sort of thing is too good to last.
This series has not only been the best of the eight played so far in this postseason, but the best in years. Two indisputably accomplished teams, each with very different approaches and without the burdens of franchise legacy, have played taut and delightful baseball replete with stuff like speed, athletic defense, rapid-response scoring, bold tactical choices, and pitching being tested but only occasionally bested. It's the stuff that makes watching your $3.9 billion investment action worth the bother of coming to the park. All that, and "Goddammit, Merrill" too.
The Padres extended the series at least a day with an incandescent 4-3 win Tuesday night, and they now trail the Brewers, the best team in the game during the regular season, 2-1 in a not-enough-games-no-matter-who-wins series. All three games have been decided by one run and hung precariously in the balance to the end. That was most thrilling in Game 2, when Brewers outfielder Jackson Chourio's walk-off hit in the gap scored two runs and stole the result from the Padres and their overpowering Padres closer Mason Miller. Because some ethereal things are happening here, Chourio opened Game 3 with a similar drive, only to have it seized before it landed by a diving San Diego center fielder Jackson Merrill, the name behind the curse.
articles.title: Padres-Brewers Has Been The Best Of October Baseball

As someone who broadly finds international breaks boring—and this current double break painfully so—I have to express gratitude to Cristiano Ronaldo for having a complete meltdown over his spot on the Portuguese national team. While his performance at the World Cup was oftentimes funny and almost always more than a little sad, this current freakout is just bizarre. OK, it’s also still pretty funny. 
The timeline: On Sept. 24, during the first game of this seemingly endless international break, Ronaldo started for Portugal against Wales in the first of four Nations League matches over the past fortnight. He played about as well as he did at the World Cup (so, not well at all), and was subbed off in the 67th minute. Readers with a decent memory might remember the minor hubbub over then-manager Roberto Martinez subbing Ronaldo out of the round of 32 match against Croatia, a match Portugal would go on to win after the substitution. That controversy had nothing with what was coming, though. 
Three days after the Wales match, Portugal played Norway in Oslo. Ronaldo did not start that game, nor did he sub on. Portugal won 2-1. Three days after that, Ronaldo left the national team camp ahead of the Oct. 1 match against Denmark (4-2 win for Portugal), and did not show up to the final match of the break on Oct. 4 against Norway again, this time in Portugal. (You know where I’m going with this: Portugal won 2-1.) In the middle of all that, Portuguese newspaper O Jogo reported that Ronaldo hadn’t just taken his ball and gone home, but had in fact, finally, retired from the national team.
articles.title: Cristiano Ronaldo Has Lost His Damn Mind

articles.author: Barry Petchesky
articles.description:
Let's play a game. What do you expect was the outcome of this 3-on-0?


Expectations are a funny thing in sports. They are as subject to the observer effect as any quantum mechanic: When a player or a team is aware of them, they may tend to play up to or exceed those expectations, or play down to them, as the case may be. Or they may be rattled and fall short. All this depends on temperament. The Maple Leafs have more observers than anyone, and their expectations are historically the least rooted in reality. Expectations and belief are two separate things, and in Toronto—at least among the 1050 caller demographic—those things are forever at war. Fans and local media believe that the Leafs will not achieve what is expected of them, even though those fans and media are the ones doing the expecting. It's a weird scene.
articles.title: Must Every Leafy Thing Be So Freighted With Meaning? Yes, Yes It Must

articles.author: Giri Nathan
articles.description:
If you listen to a certain subset of the media—not necessarily the sports media—the state of the WNBA is dire. A generational talent is being squandered. Weak leadership has failed a league on the cusp of great opportunity. Something must be done. Once we figure out what exactly that something is, it's going to get so done.
USA Today columnist Christine Brennan, who has written a book about Caitlin Clark, belongs to this subset, and has committed to viewing an entire sports league through the lens of one All-Star guard on the Indiana Fever. Clark is certainly a popular and exciting basketball player to watch, but adherence to a religiously Clarkcentric worldview can warp one's commentary over time. Eventually you come off like someone who doesn't know or care about anything else happening in the WNBA. Clark's Indiana Fever lost their first-round playoff series to the Las Vegas Aces last week, leaving Brennan to select some strained reporting angles as her book subject spun out of the postseason.
Late in Game 2 of that series, Aces star forward A'ja Wilson confronted a courtside Fever fan who she felt had "disrespected" her. "If I see a man come at me, taking steps towards me and pointing at me, I don’t give a damn what you said. I don’t give a damn how you said it, the tone. That is unacceptable," Wilson told press after the game. Brennan sought comment from the WNBA and, 36 hours later, was disappointed not to have heard back. According to her, the WNBA's slow response to queries about Wilson reflects its "leadership vacuum," and a league source's bog-standard obfuscatory description of the event is somehow a "PR nightmare."
articles.title: Christine Brennan Has Fully Lost It Over Caitlin Clark
